slides.title: Lecture 01 · Outcomes, events and counting
bullets: Experiments, outcomes and sample spaces
Events, and how to combine them
Equally likely outcomes and the axioms of probability
Counting: the multiplication rule, permutations, combinations

slides.title: Experiments and sample spaces
bullets: An experiment is any process whose result is uncertain.
An outcome is one possible result of the experiment.
The sample space Ω is the set of all possible outcomes.
The dice are told apart: (1, 6) and (6, 1) are different outcomes.

slides.title: Events
bullets: An event is a subset of the sample space.
The event E occurs when the outcome of the experiment lies in E.
Ω itself is the certain event; the empty set ∅ is the impossible event.

slides.title: Combining events
bullets: Complement E′: the outcomes not in E (E does not happen).
Union E ∪ F: the outcomes in E or F or both (at least one happens).
Intersection E ∩ F: the outcomes in both E and F (both happen).
E and F are disjoint when E ∩ F = ∅: they cannot happen together.

slides.title: Equally likely outcomes
bullets: If Ω is finite and every outcome is equally likely, then P(E) = |E| / |Ω|.
Probability becomes counting: count the event, count the sample space.
Two dice: P(sum is 7) = 6/36 = 1/6.
Two dice: P(doubles) = 6/36 = 1/6.

slides.title: The axioms of probability
bullets: Axiom 1: P(E) ≥ 0 for every event E.
Axiom 2: P(Ω) = 1.
Axiom 3: if E and F are disjoint, then P(E ∪ F) = P(E) + P(F).
Axiom 3 extends to any sequence of pairwise disjoint events.

slides.title: Consequences of the axioms
bullets: Complement rule: P(E′) = 1 − P(E).
The impossible event: P(∅) = 0.
Every probability is at most 1: P(E) ≤ 1.
Monotonicity: if E ⊆ F, then P(E) ≤ P(F).
Inclusion–exclusion: P(E ∪ F) = P(E) + P(F) − P(E ∩ F).

slides.title: The multiplication rule
bullets: A task is done in k steps, with n₁ ways to do step 1, n₂ ways to do step 2, and so on.
If the number of ways for each step does not depend on the earlier choices,
then the whole task can be done in n₁ · n₂ · n₃ · … ways, one factor per step.
A 4-digit lock code: 10 · 10 · 10 · 10 = 10,000 possible codes.
Four rolls of a die: 6⁴ = 1296 equally likely sequences.

slides.title: Permutations
bullets: n distinct objects can be put in order in n! = n · (n − 1) · … · 2 · 1 ways.
By convention 0! = 1.
Ordered selections of k from n: nPk = n · (n − 1) · … · (n − k + 1) = n! / (n − k)!.
Gold, silver and bronze among 8 runners: 8 · 7 · 6 = 336 ways.

slides.title: Combinations
bullets: Unordered selections of k from n: nCk = n! / (k! (n − k)!).
Each unordered selection appears k! times among the ordered ones: nPk = k! · nCk.
A committee of 3 from 10 people: C(10, 3) = 120.
Symmetry: C(n, k) = C(n, n − k), since choosing who is in also chooses who is out.

slides.title: Counting with cards
bullets: A standard deck has 52 cards: 4 suits of 13 ranks.
Five-card hands: C(52, 5) = 2,598,960, all equally likely after a fair shuffle.
Hands of a single suit: 4 · C(13, 5) = 5,148, probability ≈ 0.00198.
Hands holding all four aces: C(4, 4) · C(48, 1) = 48.

slides.title: At least one: count the complement
bullets: P(at least one six in four rolls) = 1 − P(no six in four rolls).
No six: 5 choices for each roll, so 5⁴ = 625 of the 1296 sequences.
Not 4 · 1/6: the events “six on roll i” overlap, so their probabilities do not add.

slides.title: Summary
bullets: Model the experiment: a sample space Ω, and events as subsets of Ω.
Equally likely outcomes: P(E) = |E| / |Ω|.
Multiply the counts of the steps; divide out orderings you do not care about.
For “at least one”, count the complement.
